{"id": "ec9511d0-f08f-4e08-88cf-fdd05d03ab63", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_AYkgFOtl87AWxbmoHKVnJ5", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the changes that could explain the symptoms, or confirm whether and when a specific change happened.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudTrail: `lookup_cloudtrail_events`\\\\n\\\\nCloudTrail calls through `use_aws` are blocked; `lookup_cloudtrail_events` is the route. It returns management events from the last 90 days, newest first, for one account and region per call.\\\\n\\\\n- Each call returns at most about 10,000 characters of events. Every event carries its full CloudTrailEvent JSON, so a call often holds only a handful of events. When it stops early it returns `continuation_timestamp`; pass that as the next `end_time` to page to older events.\\\\n- With no attribute, the tool returns only write events (`ReadOnly` is `false`), which is what a change timeline needs. LookupEvents takes one attribute per call, so passing `attribute_key` and `attribute_value` (EventSource, ResourceName, Username, EventName and so on) replaces that default, and read-only calls then share the size cap with the writes. Use an attribute to follow one resource, user or event name.\\\\n- Narrow before you page: exclude noisy event names and use windows of about 15 minutes. Excluded events do not count toward the size cap. `jmespath_filter` runs after the cap, so it shrinks the output but does not return more events.\\\\n- Passing `exclude_event_names` replaces the default exclusions (`CreateLogStream`, `Invoke`, `InvokeExecution`, `UpdateInstanceInformation`, `PutObject`); include them again if you still want them dropped.\\\\n- LookupEvents allows 2 requests per second per account and region, and one tool call may page several times, so run at most 2 CloudTrail calls at once.\\\\n- Start near the symptom onset and work backward until you find changes that address the question or have covered the requested timeframe.\\\\n\\\\nKubernetes events come from `use_kubectl`. RDS `describe_events` covers only the last 14 days; for an older window, use CloudTrail.\\\\n\\\\n## Judging a change\\\\n\\\\nA change during the incident window matters only if it relates to the investigative question or explains a symptom. When a change modified a resource that is now degraded, describe the resulting state, not just the event, and say whether that state deterministically stops the resource from working (an emptied security group, revoked IAM permissions, a black-hole route). A deterministic block takes precedence over load-based explanations, and timing alone is no reason to dismiss it.\\\\n\\\\nStop when the question is settled: you have found changes that address it, or you have covered the requested timeframe without finding any, in which case say what you searched.\\\\n\\\\nRecord each relevant change with `write_activity_observation`, including the event count and the timespan covered, unless your instructions have you state findings in your own reasoning instead.\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"references/azure.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "db0cffcb-25b5-48dc-9343-dd8a203224fb", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "The Bedrock bill didn't triple, and it wasn't a Bedrock model-token problem. Billed spend for the Bedrock service family went from about $0.40 to about $13.10 week over week, roughly 32x. That is almost entirely one 6-hour AgentCore Runtime burst on Mon 2026-11-16, triggered by a manually enabled EventBridge synthetic-traffic rule. Model-token spend fell about 89%. If the user saw "3x" somewhere, it came from a different view, account or period than I queried.

## Billed spend (Cost Explorer, daily, all three Bedrock service names; window 11-09 → 11-24 exclusive)

| Week | Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Bedrock Service | Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Total (billed) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline 11-09..11-15 | $0.4036 | $0.0006 | $0 | **≈ $0.404** |
| Last week 11-16..11-22 | $0.0453 | $0.0002 | $13.0567 | **≈ $13.10** |
| Today 11-23 (partial) | none yet | none | none | $0 |

- **Rolling last 7 days (11-17..11-23):** $0 for AgentCore, and no billed dollars for Bedrock models. The spike is a single day.
- **Coverage check:** the AgentCore total for November equals the 11-16 figure exactly, so nothing falls outside the window. 11-23 has no billed data yet.

## Ranked drivers

**1. AgentCore Runtime vCPU on 11-16: $13.0567 (billed). This is about 99.7% of the week's spend and about 100% of the increase.**
- The usage type is `USE1-Runtime:Consumption-based:vCPU`, 3.175 vCPU-hours.
- CloudWatch `AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore` `CPUUsed-vCPUHours` summed across the 5 runtimes is 3.175. It matches the billed quantity.
- Each of the 5 runtimes (`llmops_eval_orders`, `support`, `search`, `catalog` and `billing` agents) used 0.62–0.66 vCPU-hours.
- Each runtime received exactly 216 `InvokeAgentRuntime` calls, all on 11-16 and none on any other day from 11-09 to 11-23. Identical counts point to scripted traffic.
- vCPU usage by hour (UTC) on 11-16:

  | Hour | vCPU-hours |
  |---|---|
  | 09:00 | 0.10 (partial hour) |
  | 10:00–14:00 | about 0.52–0.54 per hour |
  | 15:00 | 0.43 |
  | 16:00 onward | none |

- Smaller 11-16 lines in the same service: AgentCore Gateway invocations (144 billed at $0) and regional data transfer (about $0.0000005).
- **Onset: 2026-11-16 about 09:43 UTC. End: about 15:41 UTC.**

**Trigger (confirmed by CloudTrail):**
- 09:43:49Z: `events:EnableRule` on rule `llmops-eval-synthetic-traffic`. The caller was an `Admin`-role session (alias user6, aws-cli on a laptop, app tag `kiro-ide`).
- 15:41:15Z: `events:DisableRule` on the same rule, same session.
- The rule has the schedule `rate(5 minutes)` and targets the Lambda `llmops-eval-synthetic-traffic`. It is currently DISABLED.
- About 6 hours at 5-minute intervals is about 72 firings. At 3 invocations per firing across 72 firings you get 216 per runtime, which matches. That arithmetic is my inference, not a confirmed fact.
- This explains "no deployment": it was a manual rule toggle, not a code or infrastructure change.
- Nothing in the window created any resources. I found no `CreateAgentRuntime` since 10-26, no `UpdateAgentRuntime` since 10-26, and no `CreateProvisionedModelThroughput` since 09-01.

**2. Bedrock model-token spend: down, about –$0.36 (billed).**
- Nova Lite output tokens were the only real dollar line, about $0.078 a day through 11-13. The one 11-16 reading was $0.045, and there is none after that.
- Guardrail content-policy units cost about $0.0003 a day, which is negligible.
- **Volume:** Sonnet 5 input tokens (`us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5`) were 16.5M in 11-09..11-14 against 11.3M in 11-16..11-22. Invocation counts were flat to lower. 11-23 is partial, at 1.3M input tokens and 403 invocations.
- **Other candidates checked:**
  - No model switch to a pricier model.
  - No new model IDs.
  - No new or oversized Provisioned Throughput.
  - No cross-region profile change. All traffic uses `us.` profiles, as in the baseline.
  - No tier change: the `-standard` suffix on Sonnet 5 and GPT usage types is unchanged.
  - No prompt-caching regression. The only cache usage is GPT cache-write tokens on 11-09 and 11-17.
  - No retry loop or runaway output. Per-call output size is in line with the baseline.

## Findings I could not explain (not pursued as causes)
- **Sonnet 5 and GPT tokens billed at $0.**
  - Sonnet 5 shows millions of tokens a day with `UnblendedCost` of $0. The billed quantities match CloudWatch (for example, 1,896.807K billed against 1,896,807 metered on 11-09).
  - The only record type present is `Usage`, so nothing visible explains the $0.
  - Any future price change or billing correction there could add real spend. I did not re-price these tokens.
- **AgentCore billed rate and memory.**
  - The vCPU line implies about $4.11 per vCPU-hour on 11-16, and the same on 10-27 ($30.68 for 7.46 vCPU-hours).
  - The 218.66 GB-hours of Runtime memory on 11-16 were billed at $0.
  - I did not verify these against published prices. My `pricing:GetProducts` query returned only instance-based runtime SKUs, not the consumption-based vCPU or memory rates.
- **Earlier burst.** AgentCore billed about $17.89 on 10-26 and $30.68 on 10-27 (about $48.6 together). The five runtimes were created on 10-26 (CloudTrail `CreateAgentRuntime`, by an console agentic-access session). I did not confirm what drove those days. It looks like the same pattern, hypothesis only.

## What I couldn't access or didn't do
- **Hourly Cost Explorer:** not enabled. I used CloudWatch hourly vCPU as a stand-in.
- **AgentCore control-plane read:** `ListAgentRuntimes` was denied to the agent role (`bedrock-agentcore:ListAgentRuntimes`). I had no runtime configuration details such as CPU, memory or idle timeouts.
- **Lambda and rule details:** I did not read the Lambda's code or configuration, so I don't know what payload it sends.
- **Invocation logging:** it is enabled to a CloudWatch log group (`/llmops-demo/bedrock-invocations`). I didn't query it, because the model-token side shows no anomaly. Per-caller attribution of model spend is therefore not done.
- **Bedrock Agents, Knowledge Bases and OpenSearch:** I saw only read-only KB list calls by the monitoring role. I didn't check KB/OpenSearch costs separately. Cost Explorer showed no Bedrock Service or OpenSearch-related spike under the Bedrock names. I did not check an OpenSearch service line.
- **Cost Explorer scope:** it is account-wide and shows only this account. I did not check other regions.

## Recommended next steps
1. **Confirm the intent** with the person behind the Admin session. Was the 11-16 run of `llmops-eval-synthetic-traffic` a planned eval or load test? If it recurs, the cost is roughly $13 per 6 hours across the 5 runtimes (billed rate, not independently price-checked).
2. **Guard against repeat runs.** Add an AWS Budgets alert, or a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor, scoped to `Amazon Bedrock AgentCore`. Tag the runtimes and the rule.
3. **Review the runtimes.** If the evals are done, check whether the runtimes need to stay deployed. They bill only when used, so keeping them mostly costs nothing.
4. **Ask AWS Billing about the $0 lines.** That means Sonnet 5 tokens and AgentCore memory. Ask whether they are free-tier, credit-related or not yet rated.
5. **Grant read access if you want more.** Allow `bedrock-agentcore:ListAgentRuntimes` and `GetAgentRuntime` on the agent role, and enable hourly Cost Explorer granularity from the payer account. I can then work out per-runtime configuration and cost.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
